articles.title: Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us
articles.summary: TP-Link has signed a letter of intent to manufacture routers in Mississippi — in an attempt to get the FCC to approve its Wi-Fi 8 routers for import and sale.
articles.body: TP-Link, one of the world’s leading manufacturers of consumer Wi-Fi routers, is in a precarious position in the US. The company just launched its first Wi-Fi 8 routers, but can’t bring them here because of President Donald Trump’s foreign router ban. Even though competitors Netgear and Asus make their routers in Asia, they’ve mysteriously obtained blanket waivers for all their new gear; perhaps because of alleged ties to China, TP-Link hasn’t managed to get such a waiver yet. But TP-Link is willing to do something those companies weren’t — to invest nearly $1 billion to make routers in the United States, creating “hundreds of high-paying research and development, manufacturing, and construction jobs for American workers over the next four years,” according to a letter TP-Link sent to the FCC. This week, it announced a letter of intent with US contract manufacturer Key Tronic to begin “domestic assembly” of its Wi-Fi 8 routers in Corinth, Mississippi. It could begin producing routers “as early as next year.” Intriguingly, this might not just be slapping boards into a plastic box. “If you look at what we do with the products in Vietnam, you’ve got raw components coming in and you’ve got completed, tested, shrink-wrapped products coming out,” TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky tells The Verge. “You’ve got surface-mount technology, many layers of testing quality control, we’re doing plastic injection molding, and as far as I know that is what we intend to do in Mississippi.” But how likely is that “letter of intent” to turn into a true manufacturing plant? After talking to Kovsky, it sounds like the stars might need to align. What is TP-Link waiting for? A deal with the Federal Communications Commission. Kovksy confirms the offer hinges on the FCC granting that router ban waiver — formally known as “conditional approval” — before it can proceed. Kovsky wouldn’t tell me how long ago TP-Link applied for that waiver, but it sounds like the FCC hasn’t yet given the company any idea whether it’ll be approved. TP-Link had to provide lots of info about the company’s structure, ownership, and supply chain, but Kovksy confirms the FCC hasn’t asked any follow-up questions about other topics, and he says the FCC doesn’t exactly tell companies when it denies conditional approval. “We’re looking at offering total transparency to these agencies, and we’re open to negotiations,” he says. “Nothing is written in stone.” Why does TP-Link need an import waiver if it’ll be building routers in the US? “I have asked that question myself,” Kovsky tells The Verge. The short answer is components. Even though TP-Link buys its chipsets from US companies like Qualcomm and Broadcom, those companies don’t actually produce those chips in the US. “Do they count as US product?” Kovsky rhetorically asks. “It’s not a lock, and we would rather have [the waiver],” he says. Why might the FCC hesitate? Five states have now sued over TP-Link’s alleged ties to China, and many more are directly asking the FCC not to grant a waiver, claiming the company dominates the consumer router market, that it’s a Chinese company posing as a US one, that the routers have brought serious security vulnerabilities into US homes, and more. Kovksy suggests it’s all based on misinformation, even the company’s market share: “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three. It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.” TP-Link’s website clarifies that it has 10 percent market share when you count all the routers that internet providers put into people’s homes. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever. We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category to my knowledge,” Kovsky says. It’s certainly true that Netgear routers got a blanket waiver despite being similarly implicated in some security scandals and Chinese hacks. I’ll say it once more: The router ban isn’t about security. If it gets the waiver, does TP-Link intend to produce all US-bound routers in the US? TP-Link is not willing to commit to that yet. “I don’t think that’s entirely determined,” Kovksy says. “Some of that is going to be: What are the FCC and the administration really trying to achieve?” The administration already has a stated goal, though: It wants Made-in-USA products where at least 65 percent of their components are also made here. Kovsky says that TP-Link would be “happy to comply with that, to the extent that it can continue to produce products that meet its criteria for quality and affordability.” “That is going to be challenging, certainly in the short term, [because] those components for the most part just are not produced in the US,” Kovsky says. He says TP-Link believes components will become more available and affordable if the US pushes other manufacturers to invest, but the waiver isn’t the only factor in its decision. If it gets the waiver, will TP-Link invest, or will it need to find an inexpensive source of components or other things before it can go ahead? “I think those are probably going to be business decisions that the CEO will ultimately have to make,” Kovksy begins. “Well, I hope he doesn’t have to make those decisions, frankly, that everything falls in line. He is very committed to making this investment,” he says. Notably, TP-Link would not confirm Kovsky’s suggestion that it might completely manufacture routers in the US and only source the raw components. I told the company that if I could say TP-Link was committed to anything other than “final assembly,” it’d be well worth sharing with readers. “At this stage, TP-Link is not sharing specific job numbers or detailed technical details of the assembly process beyond what’s in today’s press release,” third-party spokesperson Ricca Silverio told me. I don’t think this is Foxconn in Wisconsin all over again because TP-Link probably won’t get its conditional approval, let alone invest in empty buildings. Foreign gadget bans from President Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr seem explicitly designed to target companies China hawks claim to be worried about, like DJI or Unitree, while letting favored companies through. But the hawks, including a coalition of congresspeople led by Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), seem to hate TP-Link, too.

articles.title: Judge orders Meta to pay New Mexico $25B in Cambridge Analytica case
articles.summary: A judge in New Mexico ordered the technology giant Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for misleading users about its privacy and content policies. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez (D) announced the judge’s order Wednesday, calling it “one of the single largest — if not the largest —…
articles.body:
A judge in New Mexico ordered the technology giant Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for misleading users about its privacy and content policies.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez (D) announced the judge’s order Wednesday, calling it “one of the single largest — if not the largest — single state verdict against the company in American history.”

“Today’s judgement from a state, which admittedly is not very big in terms of population, should be a clear warning to everyone in Big Tech, Mr. [Mark] Zuckerberg, Meta, social media companies, indeed AI companies,” Torrez said at a press conference.

The order from Santa Fe Judge Francis Mathew comes just weeks after jurors found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws when the British consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested data from Facebook users for political ads during the 2016 election.

Following an expected appeals process, Torrez said the payment from Meta will be put toward public education in the state.

New Mexico was one of just two states that chose not to join the 48-state settlement with Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. The company agreed to pay $459 million as part of that settlement.

Attorneys for New Mexico originally sought $35 billion to $40 billion, suggesting the order would need to impact Meta’s stock price to establish real change, The Associated Press reported. Meta’s lawyers argued to pay no more than $3.4 billion, claiming anything more than $34 billion would violate due process.

Torrez told reporters he expects Meta to appeal, but New Mexico intends “to do everything in our power to make sure that those resources are eventually delivered” to the state.

“The fact that we received a judgment today that is less than the total statutory max shouldn’t be mistaken for the larger message,” Torrez said, adding the previously settled states “are sharing $459 million for the conduct at issue, and New Mexico just received a $25 billion judgement.”

“So I’ll leave it to you to determine whether and to what extent that counts as a victory,” he told reporters.

Wednesday’s order is the latest in a string of legal battles over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The Supreme Court in 2024 heard Facebook’s bid to block a shareholder lawsuit over the Cambridge Analytica data scandal from moving forward.

Shareholders sued the social media company after the public became widely aware of the scandal in 2018, accusing Facebook of misleading investors in an earlier securities filing by failing to mention Cambridge Analytica’s misuse of user data.

While the tech giant acknowledged in a 2016 filing that improper third-party use of its data could harm its business, it did not mention Cambridge Analytica. As a result, the shareholders argue, they were led to believe that no such incident had occurred.

Facebook argued its statements in the risk disclosure section of the securities filing were only about future events and did not suggest that such an event had never taken place.

The Supreme Court later dismissed the case without issuing a ruling on the merits.

articles.title: UN climate report says world will fail 1.5-degree Paris goal but argues for keeping overshoot brief
articles.summary: A new United Nations climate report released Wednesday said that while global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5-degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, urgent and steep cuts to emissions can help reduce the overshoot. The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return published by the U.N. Environment Programme, looks at the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, in…
articles.body:
A new United Nations climate report released Wednesday said that while global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5-degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, urgent and steep cuts to emissions can help reduce the overshoot.

The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return published by the U.N. Environment Programme , looks at the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, in which peak warming can be limited to 1.7-1.8 degrees Celsius in the middle of the century, according to a press release from the U.N.

“The chance to keep global warming below 1.5°C with no overshoot is gone,” the UNEP wrote in a post on social platform X. “But urgent action can still limit the overshoot and bring warming back to 1.5°C by 2100.”

To achieve the target of limiting overshoot and returning to the 1.5-degree Celsius target laid out in the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, global greenhouse gas emissions would have to be reduced by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040, relative to 2025 levels, according to a press release from UNEP .

“By contrast, the full implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) would only reduce emissions by 5-8 per cent by 2030 and 11-15 per cent by 2035, relative to 2025 levels,” the release said.

The report found that if countries follow their current policies, warming levels could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius within the century and increase after. If all existing emissions reduction pledges are fulfilled, warming would be limited to 2.6 degrees Celsius, projections that the UNEP said are “are worse than last year’s projections due to the withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions.”

Earlier this year in January , President Trump’s move to pull the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement took effect. The president signed an executive order to withdraw U.S. from the agreement soon after he took office last year. Trump, in his first term, also withdrew the U.S. from the agreement before former President Biden rejoined the pact.

In the U.N. release, UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen warned that every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5 degrees Celsius increases the chance of climate impacts and risks.

She pointed to “the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year.”

“So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century”, she said.

articles.title: Rubio: NFL game in Paris will be ‘fine’ despite riots

articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio says he’s not worried about the safety of NFL players, coaches and fans in France, where the league will play a game on Sunday amid widespread rioting across the country.

“Our embassy feels the game will be fine,” Rubio told OutKick and Fox News Digital . “We have no indication the game will be impacted in any way.”

“I was never planning to go anyways,” he added of the game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints, slated for 9 a.m. EDT at Stade de France near Paris.

France has been hit by widespread political protests in recent days, some of which have devolved into violent rioting and looting in major cities.

Many on the political right in the U.S. have blamed the social unrest in France on immigration and pointed to it as a result of progressive ideology run amok.

The NFL, meanwhile, is playing a record 11 games overseas this season as the most popular U.S. sports league works to grow its brand internationally.

The league has already staged games in London, Australia and Brazil, with more slated before the regular season concludes in December.

articles.title: NSA warns organizations to patch security flaws identified by AI
articles.summary: The National Security Agency (NSA) warned organizations Wednesday to immediately patch a pair of security flaws or take their systems offline after artificial intelligence discovered vulnerabilities in a key programming language. “Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities,” the NSA’s cyber…
articles.body:
The National Security Agency (NSA) warned organizations Wednesday to immediately patch a pair of security flaws or take their systems offline after artificial intelligence discovered vulnerabilities in a key programming language.

“Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities,” the NSA’s cyber division wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the agency continued. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

PHP is a programming language frequently used in web development and is often referred to as the “backbone of the web.” It powers 70 percent of all websites around the world, including popular platforms like WordPress and Wikipedia’s MediaWiki.

The cyber division of the FBI similarly urged organizations to act quickly and users to monitor web services for suspicious activity. Users were told to report “signs of compromise” to a local FBI field office or the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Developers of the PHP language released fixes to the vulnerabilities Wednesday morning after government websites in Europe and elsewhere went dark, urging users to “update immediately.”

The bug identified by security researchers has been present in the code for 14 years, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said Wednesday.

A limited version of the bug was initially discovered in 2024 but wasn’t deemed significant, he noted. In August, security researchers working with an OpenAI initiative and using the company’s GPT-5.6 Sol model found a version of the vulnerability.

“Over the past two months, we have been leading a coalition to mitigate one of the most severe bugs in open source software found in recent memory,” Brockman wrote on X.

“This vulnerability allows any attacker to execute code on nearly all deployed PHP application, effectively allowing them to exfiltrate private user data or modifying the site however they want,” he added.

OpenAI also released a PHP version checker within its Codex system to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions.

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in malware history,” researchers at Wiz wrote in a blog post Wednesday.

AI developers have often touted the technology’s ability to spot security vulnerabilities at significantly faster rates than humans or traditional computer systems, while warning the same tools can also be employed by bad actors.

articles.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties over the Cambridge Analytica scandal
articles.summary: A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading the public about its privacy and misinformation measures stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
articles.body: The Cambridge Analytica scandal has come back to haunt Meta after a New Mexico judge ordered it to pay $25 billion in penalties for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law. The ruling marks the biggest legal hit Meta has taken this year, even as it’s faced several other losses or settlements. A New Mexico jury ruled in September that Meta misled consumers over how it protected their data and prevented misinformation and hate speech on its platforms. The case stemmed from a 2021 complaint in the wake of the revelations a few years earlier that UK political consultancy Cambridge Analytica harvested data from millions of Facebook accounts to pinpoint messages that would resonate with voters leading up to President Donald Trump’s first election. The judge found that the “extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership,” and other factors justified the highest penalty allowed under the law, at $5,000 per violation. That brings the total civil penalties to more than $219 billion, but the judge reduced it to $25 billion. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Even this smaller sum is “one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in U.S. history,” according to the AG’s office, and dwarfs other recent rulings and settlements involving Meta. In another landmark ruling in New Mexico state court, Meta was ordered to pay a total of nearly $1 billion in civil penalties and abatement for misleading the public about the safety of its products. In a separate agreement with most other state AGs, Meta settled an array of kids online safety complaints for $17.1 billion — but $5.3 billion of that is contingent on YouTube and TikTok installing similar measures. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez issued a triumphant statement after the latest in his string of wins against Meta (though the company managed to fight off many of the business changes the AG asked for in the remedies portion of the kids online safety case). “This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,” Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law.” Update, October 21st: Added statement from Meta.

articles.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From AI-discovered PHP vulnerabilities to flaws in Node.js and popular AI tool LiteLLM, cybersecurity teams have plenty to worry about this week.
articles.body:
The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline , Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP . The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js , the open-source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub , and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted.

The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems.

LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided.

And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised , potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed .” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library).

These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August.

Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered.

articles.title: GM is betting compute and AI will help it compete with Chinese automakers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: To compete with Tesla, Rivian, and a host of Chinese automakers, GM’s fourth-gen EV platform will roll out a new central computer and electrical architecture that will debut in 2028 in the Cadillac Escalade IQ.
articles.body:
When GM announced its new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday, what the automaker didn’t share was almost as notable as what it did.

The new EV platform, part of a series of technology-focused announced during its annual GM Forward event in New York, didn’t talk about suspension geometries, dash-to-axle ratios, and torsional rigidity, all nerdy automotive terms that translate to how people will experience a car. Is it supple or sporty? Does it have a refined stance? When it hits a pothole, does it feel like a bank vault or a paper plate?

Instead, GM’s announcement centered on novel battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and an entirely new central computing platform and electrical architecture that will connect every system in the car, including acceleration and power, steering, braking, and active safety features as well as software. Lots and lots of software.

“We think vehicles can become a more capable and helpful part of everyday life if we make them spaces that understand context, reduce friction, and give people back moments that would otherwise be consumed by the demands of the road,” Sterling Anderson, executive vice president, global product, and chief product officer at GM, told TechCrunch in a recent interview.

That sure doesn’t sound like a traditional automaker’s pitch. Then again, since the arrival of Tesla, Rivian, and Chinese automakers, the industry hasn’t been the same. Ride and handling still matter, but they’re table stakes. What sets vehicles apart today is largely defined by software.

Anderson has talked about this future GM before. Last year, the company announced plans to overhaul the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant.

This year, GM is providing more details and dates. This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also rollout an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over.

European and U.S. automakers have spent years chasing the prospect of software-defined vehicles, but have often fallen short. Volkswagen Group had so much trouble with its own in-house effort, including its troubled Cariad unit, that it struck a $5.8 billion joint venture deal with relative newcomer Rivian.

GM has been on its own capitally intensive software adventure. The company has bet heavily on software in recent years. It ditched the popular smartphone projection technology Apple CarPlay for nearly all of its EVs, and instead turned to a Google-based infotainment system, which is actually quite capable even if it doesn’t yet live up to the standards set by Tesla and Rivian.

It’s poured billions into software and autonomous vehicle technology development too. GM’s capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million, which gives a sense of how much it is spending even as it spreads out the cost over years.

Like many legacy automakers, GM has come to the conclusion that the old approach to electronics, which scattered computer chips throughout the vehicle, was holding it back.

For fourth-generation EVs, GM will centralize much of those functions on a Central Compute Unit (CCU) that’s 40-times more powerful than its existing systems. Eliminating smaller chips on the edges will help trim wiring by 30%, saving weight and simplifying assembly.

GM notes that this new CCU will work on fossil fuel models, too, though it will debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a vehicle that is shaping up to be the automaker’s technological flagship.

The CCU will handle the usual propulsion and chassis controls, but also perception and active safety. That should help pave the way for more advanced autonomy features, which GM also announced on Wednesday.

Such a move was perhaps inevitable. Pressure on automakers has been building on all sides.

Domestically, Tesla has been pushing the boundaries of autonomy, in part because it developed a true software-defined vehicle.

Automakers like GM are also feeling pressure from Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years, down from the usual four to five years.

GM intends to match that cadence. Alongside announcements about battery chemistries and autonomy, GM outlined how enterprise AI tools have sped up vehicle development across every sector as it pushes to slash its traditional four-to-five-year development timeline in half.

GM gave a brief glimpse of its revamped development strategy. One example: engineers went through 300,000 virtual designs of a new lithium-manganese-rich battery pack before they assembled the first physical prototype. That helped the concept move to an approved program in one month.

Such speed will help GM save costs as it races to preserve profitability amid a historic upheaval in the automotive industry. But will it be enough to catapult it back into the leadership position it once enjoyed?

The rise of Chinese automakers won’t make it easy. Their factories are capable of producing far more than Chinese consumers can absorb, and coupled with government subsidies and cheaper labor, these vehicles have flooded markets from Europe to South America with inexpensive vehicles.

Chinese automaker’s cost advantage is so steep that, without trade barriers, “they will pretty much demolish most other companies in the world,” Elon Musk said in a 2024 earnings call. In response, he has been trying to pivot Tesla from an automotive company to an AI and robotics company.

GM’s move into autonomy signals a similar shift. But to deliver true autonomy, GM realized it didn’t have the platform it needed. With a new architecture, it should have a fighting chance.

articles.title: PHP: The three letters that shut down sites all over the internet today
articles.summary: Patches have been released to fix the AI-discovered “PHP2Shell” issue, but with millions of servers potentially vulnerable, the race is on to apply the updates and secure data.
articles.body: Two bugs found with AI are behind major issues today for 4chan, DeviantArt, Wikipedia, and the blog where the bar around the corner posts pictures of people’s dogs. The “critical vulnerabilities” were discovered in the PHP programming language, which underpins much of the internet, including any site built on WordPress. But it’s far bigger than that. Some Dutch and Finnish government agencies took their sites down as a precaution. The NSA Cybersecurity account on X recommended that organizations take their systems offline if “an immediate update is not feasible,” as did the UK’s National Cyber Security Center. Even Pokémon Home and Pokémon Champions were taken offline, Kotaku reports. The vulnerability isn’t exactly new. It’s been present in PHP for roughly 20 years, but exploiting it “required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” according to security firm Wiz. However, powerful AI models have made it much easier to turn that kind of obscure bug into dangerous vulnerabilities. As a casual internet user, you might be wondering what exactly the barrage of jargon like “RCE via OOM corruption” means, how concerned you should be, and how exactly a vulnerability this severe flew under the radar for so long. What is PHP? W3Techs, a survey service, says that the PHP programming language is used by “69.3 percent of all the websites whose server-side programming language we know,” including popular sites like Wikipedia and WordPress. The internet security site VirusTotal says its scanner currently registers about 3.8 million sites running PHP with at least one port open. What happened? According to OpenAI, an AI security group called Calif identified a “critical” PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz independently discovered and reported the vulnerabilities using AI. The PHP Foundation says that an exploit for one of the vulnerabilities “was theorized” in 2024, but “no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.” Now the PHP Group says hackers could use the two vulnerabilities for “unauthenticated remote code execution,” like running their own code, changing content, and accessing a site’s stored data without needing an administrator login or password. > RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. > RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. How serious is it? Very. The PHP Group says that basically any site running PHP is at risk. OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research, said: “We consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” And Wiz said it’s “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered … in software history.” Last night, the CTO of Cloudflare said that it was “seeing early attacks emerging.” It’s hard to understate just how bad this could get. The vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to take full control of a server. That includes gaining access to passwords, API keys, cryptographic certificates, and databases of sensitive information. They could also execute code on those servers, turning them into vectors to attack other vulnerable servers. And, thanks to AI, it’s relatively trivial for a determined hacker to exploit these flaws now that they have been revealed. What can I do? As a user, not much. The vulnerability affects servers running PHP and doesn’t necessarily target users directly, but it could use compromised sites to spread malware and steal other valuable data. If you’re feeling extra cautious, check the social accounts of sites and services you frequently use to see if they’ve posted any updates before visiting. If you have a website, even a simple blog, it’s time to check what version of PHP your site uses, if any. If you’re using a service like Squarespace or Wix, you’re in the clear, as those don’t support PHP. Customers of Hostinger, GoDaddy, Bluehost, or other web hosting services should be more cautious. GoDaddy says that any site using PHP should assume it is affected and update to the fixed release as soon as possible. It also says that sites running PHP 8.1 or older should upgrade to a newer version, as they’re no longer supported and there will not be an official fix coming. Those on a managed hosting service should check with their provider to see when they should expect the fix to be deployed. If you sell products or services or have any sensitive data on your servers at all, it’s best to disable your site until your host patches their version of PHP.

Major hostilities brewing? US orders departure of some embassy staff, families from Gulf region

The State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as the Iranian-backed Houthis have continued to attack the country.

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly , including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority , and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them as they return to the U.S.,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Reuters reported Wednesday that the U.S. government is preparing to issue an ordered departure of some personnel and family members from U.S. embassies across the Gulf .

And The Agence France-Presse later reported that the U.S. ordered families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain to leave, citing a diplomatic source.

Asked about the reports, Trump feigned ignorance, telling journalist: “I don’t know that they are. You are telling me something — I wouldn’t know that .”

The new order comes as the Houthis are engaged in a war against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and have been attacking infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia , including civilian airports and other critical sites that have led to civilian casualties.

Saudi Arabia’s air defense intercepted a drone targeting Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday, but two people were killed and another two were injured from the falling debris, the nation’s energy ministry said.
